headlines.article_text: Tesla (TSLA) Q3 2026 earnings report Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. Automotive revenue fell 3% from a year earlier. Tesla shares are down 14% this year, underperforming the rest of megacap tech. In this article TSLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 0:48 00:48 Tesla beats on Q3 revenue and earnings expectations Closing Bell: Overtime Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday, even as automotive revenue dropped. The stock was little changed in extended trading. Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: Earnings per share: 48 cents adjusted vs. 43 cents estimated Revenue: $28.05 billion vs. $27.9 billion estimated Tesla's earnings report lands a day after CEO Elon Musk told investors on SpaceX's quarterly call that it would be a "good idea" for his two companies to merge, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up. "I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the call, responding to a question about a potential merger. "Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this." On the Tesla side, that means needing a 50% vote of all shares, which is "quite a high hurdle," he said. Revenue was down slightly flat from a year earlier, when the company generated sales of $28.24 billion, Tesla said in its earnings deck. In Tesla's core automotive business, revenue declined 3% from a year earlier to $20.56 billion in the quarter. Energy revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion. Balancing out the declines were gains in Tesla's services and other revenue. Sales there climbed 33% from a year ago to $4.61 billion. Tesla blamed its lackluster automotive revenue and profits on lower average sales prices for its cars during the quarter, and trouble securing battery supplies to make enough vehicles to fulfill a backlog of orders. Net income attributable to common share holders plummeted 29% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, from $1.11 billion, or 32 cents a year earlier, Tesla said. The drop in profitability reflects a surge in spending on robotics and artificial intelligence initiatives. Capital expenditures more than doubled from a year earlier to $3.73 billion. Free cash flow plunged by 62% year over year to $1.53 billion, after Tesla turned free cash flow negative in the second quarter. A Tesla Bot, also known as Optimus, is displayed beside Tesla logos at a promotional exhibition in a shopping mall on September 18, 2026, in Hong Kong, China. Cheng Xin | Getty Images Tesla said uptake of its FSD (Supervised), a partially automated driving system the company sells for $99 per month in the U.S., grew by 20 percentage points from the second quarter. Active FSD subscriptions increased 67% from a year earlier to 1.74 million. "We believe that FSD is driving demand in markets where it is available, and we continue to work with regulators to get it approved in other markets," the company said in its investor deck. Tesla said its auto sales in Canada, Japan, Taiwan and Australia hit new records during the quarter. However, the company has gotten meager growth out of its core market of late as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit. Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications. One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas. That partnership with SpaceX along with other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, fueled intensifying speculation that Musk's companies were on the verge of combining in what would be a historic transaction. Tesla executives will update investors on a conference call at 5:30 p.m. ET. headlines.title: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike and stock sinks
headlines.summary: CoreWeave shares are down 29% in October, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening.
headlines.article_text: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike, stock sinks Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CoreWeave's stock is down 29% this month, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening. The company's elevated bond yield is prompting investors to question what additional financing options are available. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients this week, referring to AI bonds. In this article CRWV Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator appears after the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on March 28, 2025. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors. With interest rates spiking and AI buildout concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis." CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $34 billion, with its stock down 29% this month. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%. CoreWeave's stock move this month The spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 164% in the past year and 30% in October. It last stood at nearly 1,067 basis points, or 10.67%. CoreWeave declined to comment. The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 27% this month, while IREN's stock is down 32%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned IPO, citing market volatility and conditions. U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month. A representative from Nscale declined to comment. On hold until midterms CoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft . That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing. Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing. "Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio Management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview. watch now VIDEO 2:39 02:39 CoreWeave falls amid AI debt fears Power Lunch CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options. "Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant." CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet. One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027. "Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter." Another question is whether Nvidia step in if necessary? Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement. While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Analysts at Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase and Barclays have put out bullish notes on the company this week, highlighting the company's GPU-backed loans and its solid list of investment grade customers like Microsoft and Meta . Goldman analysts emphasized the company's strength in the market relative to many of its neocloud competitors. "Not all neoclouds are created equal," they wrote, in upgrading their rating to buy from hold. "CoreWeave is likely in the top quartile of neoclouds, if not the top decile, when measured on performance and ability to execute." —CNBC's Michelle Fox and Jordan Novet contributed to this report. Kevin Carter | Getty Images News | Getty Images Southwest Airlines became the third major U.S. airline this month to cut its 2026 profit forecast due to higher fuel prices, but CEO Bob Jordan said travelers continue to book despite higher fares. The carrier expects to earn between $2.60 and $2.85 a share on an adjusted basis this year, down from its forecast in July of between $3.25 to as much as $4.25 a share. Here's what Southwest reported for third quarter compared with Wall Street expectations, according to consensus estimates from LSEG: Earnings per share: 66 cents adjusted vs. 58 cents expected Revenue: $8.42 billion adjusted vs. $8.25 billion expected Southwest forecast per-share adjusted earnings of between 55 cents and 80 cents in the fourth quarter and unit revenue, a gauge of airfare, up as much as 21% from a year earlier. It said it expects to grow capacity by up to 4% year over year. "Demand remained strong as we lapped last year's bag fee and other commercial initiatives, reinforcing our belief that the earnings power we've built is durable, even with significantly higher fuel costs," Jordan said in an earnings release. The airline said its average passenger fare was $231.69 in the third quarter, up almost 27% from the same quarter of 2025. A spokesman said that number does not include add-on fees. The number of revenue passengers carried fell 3.2% to 33.47 million people. Under pressure to grow revenue, Southwest has been remaking its longtime business model over the past several years, scrapping its old policies like two free checked bags per passenger and open seating. In its place, Southwest has started charging for many seat assignments and added a bag fee, similar to major competitors. For the third quarter, Southwest posted net income of $270 million, or 55 cents a share, up from $54 million or 10 cents a share a year earlier. Revenue rose more than 21% to $8.42 billion. Adjusting for one-time items, Southwest reported 66 cents a share. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines also cut their profit outlooks for the rest of the year when they reported third-quarter earnings. headlines.article_text: GM aims to shorten vehicle development time with AI, software push Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points General Motors is hoping to reduce the time it takes to develop vehicles, targeting a roughly two-year cycle as it expands its use of artificial intelligence, simulation and vehicle software. GM says it is using artificial intelligence, simulation and more concurrent engineering to shorten development and reduce physical testing. The automaker is also expanding in-vehicle AI and plans to introduce eyes-off highway driving beginning with the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. In this article GM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:20 04:20 Highlights from GM Forward 2026 Power Lunch NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market. The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half. GM also reconfirmed that by 2028 , it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models. "All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan. The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers. "Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal. The event comes as Chinese automakers are growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage. GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities . Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses. He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad. "There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise." Next-generation vehicles GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines. The company said those coming vehicles — regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems. That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features. The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs. CEO and Chair of General Motors Mary Barra delivers a speech during the brand's annual technology event in New York on Oct. 21, 2026. Charly Triballeau | AFP | Getty Images GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact. GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling back billions of dollars in investments in EVs , it remains committed to producing them. "We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them." AI development GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development. The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed. "This concurrent engineering model allows us to innovate faster, improve continuously, and scale new technologies across our lineup with incredible agility," the company said in a release. From left, GM CEO Mary Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and President Mark Reuss at the company's GM Forward event in downtown Manhattan on Oct. 21, 2026. Michael Wayland | CNBC GM used the development of its next-generation vehicles, including a new battery chemistry, as an example of how the new technologies are reshaping its vehicle development. The company said it virtually tested more than 300,000 battery designs using its recently announced lithium manganese rich battery chemistry, or LMR, before building a single physical prototype. Anderson said Wednesday that LMR will be the exclusive battery tech for its fourth-generation EVs. GM had previously said it wanted to use those batteries in full-size electric vehicles such as its Chevrolet Silverado and Escalade IQ beginning in 2028. Anderson said GM is uniquely positioned to use AI compared to other automotive companies because of its more than 100 years in the industry as well as 30 years of OnStar. "In the age of AI, data is currency," Anderson said. "For decades, GM's engineering, manufacturing and product teams have generated unparalleled body of data that we're now using to build industry-leading AI tools." In-vehicle AI The company is building on its internal use of AI to better shape its experiences for customers. GM on Wednesday reconfirmed that it plans to launch a proprietary in-vehicle AI assistant through its OnStar technology brand. The OnStar AI assistant is expected to launch in the coming months on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV through an over-the-air update before expanding to other models. GM currently uses Google's Gemini for its in-vehicle AI assistant. The company told CNBC earlier this year that the GM-developed AI will be more integrated with the vehicle. The goal for OnStar AI, which will be available through a subscription, is to help customers be productive while in the car, especially if the vehicle has self-driving capabilities that don't require the driver or passengers to monitor the system. A New Mexico district court judge said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. Brendan McDermid | Reuters Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences." Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal." "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." Read more CNBC tech news Meta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reaction Tesla beats on earnings and sales even as auto revenue declines Intel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind schedule Investors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance. Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal. headlines.article_text: Rick Rieder sees historic opportunity in investment-grade bonds Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points BlackRock's Rick Rieder is bullish on this area of the credit market for the first time in a "long time." The CIO of global fixed income lays out his fourth-quarter fixed-income outlook in an exclusive interview. In this article BLK Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Rick Rieder speaking at the CNBC CEO Council Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 2, 2026. Aaron Clamage | CNBC Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview. Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration. "Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook , released Wednesday. That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance." While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus. The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC) , which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit. iShares Flexible Income Active ETF year to date Best opportunities include hyperscalers Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3. That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet , Amazon , Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG. "They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it." Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July , that stood at 8.5%. That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised. "Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield." Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names. "There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be." The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out. Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle , which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits. CoreWeave's 2031 bond yield on Oct. 21, 2026 Fed watch Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve , which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool . The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said. "They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure." Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added. Calculating risks ahead Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026. "The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said. Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched. "With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on." In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said. headlines.summary: Elon Musk’s planned SpaceX share gift through Trump Accounts could be the start of a broader philanthropic push, says Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner.
headlines.article_text: Musk's Trump Account SpaceX stock is 'tip of the iceberg': Gerstner Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points In an X post on Monday, Elon Musk said that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year. Brad Gerstner, founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, said on Wednesday that the gift would go to Trump Accounts in an exclusive interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "Elon is the tip of the iceberg," said Gerstner. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:47 06:47 Brad Gerstner on Trump Accounts: One of the most successful changes to our social contract in 100 years Squawk Box Elon Musk said earlier this week that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year, and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner said Wednesday that the stock donations would come via Trump Accounts . If it happens, that donation of $10.5 billion worth of shares is just the beginning, according to Gerstner, the founder of Invest America and an architect of Trump Accounts, the new tax-deferred investing accounts for children. "Elon is the tip of the iceberg," Gerstner told CNBC's "Squawk Box" in an exclusive interview on Wednesday. "This is the most giving country on the planet," he said. "I told the president, I think I can raise $100 billion over the course of the next 12 months to sponsor all of the kids in America." In addition to Musk, Gerstner said he had also talked to "every major tech CEO and founder." A $100 billion fundraising target would represent about one-sixth of all U.S. charitable giving. Americans donated $592.5 billion in 2024, according to the latest data from the National Philanthropic Trust . Gerstner has committed about $35 million to help seed the investment accounts for kids in his home state of Indiana. Read more CNBC personal finance coverage CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approach Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations Thousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher payments Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September, which allow Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a change from previous guidelines that only allowed diversified, low-cost index funds . "The Treasury targeted this carve-out at mega-donors and large philanthropic foundations, such as the Dells, who made a multibillion-dollar charitable pledge," said Adam Bergman, founder of IRA Financial and a tax attorney based in Miami. "It allows them to donate large blocks of publicly traded stock without triggering substantial capital-gains taxes." The move to permit stock donations could pave the way for more large-scale gifts, and a number of other philanthropists are poised to participate, Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano also told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Oct. 8. "They range from small to mega," he said. "We do have mega donors in the nine-digit range, you know, bunches of them." In the broader world of charitable giving, Treasury's temporary regulations also give donors unusual influence over children's investments , according to lawyers and philanthropic experts who spoke with CNBC. Future Trump Account expansion "As @TrumpAccounts continues to grow we look forward to more philanthropists joining the movement and helping children across America jumpstart their financial future," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in an X post Monday . The latest Trump Account comments come weeks after the Treasury Department auto-enrolled more than 60 million children . Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts , are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number. Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also claim a one-time $ 1,000 pilot program contribution from the Treasury. Gerstner also said Wednesday that there is a push to expand access to the accounts to all U.S. citizens under age 40. "Why not pull forward 20 years of IRAs? We can create all of those today," he said. "So if Elon says then, I want to give to everyone under 40, or OpenAI says I want to give to everyone under 40, there's a vehicle, there's a vessel that they can start compounding in ... those are the types of things we are working on." In addition to more than 70 million children under 18 in the U.S., about 90 million U.S. citizens are between 18 and 40 years of age, according to CNBC's analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data. However, expanding Trump Accounts to Americans under age 40 would require a legislative change from Congress. In an X post on Tuesday , Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, called the proposed expansion a "game-changer," and said he would "lead the bill in the Senate to make it happen." Gerstner told CNBC on Wednesday that expanding the Trump Account age limit is "wildly popular" among congressional Democrats and Republicans. But it's unclear whether the proposal has the legislative backing needed to become law.
